Volume One:
Introduction and Structural Analysis.
The *Lülu Jizhu* (Brief Record of the Master’s Transmission) by the Fifth Patriarch;
the *Faxiang Shu* (Numerical Account of Dharmalakṣaṇa); and the *Zhenwang Shengmie Faxiang Tu* (Diagram of the Phenomenal Characteristics of True and False Arising and Ceasing), one fascicle.
Preface to the Commentary on the Two Treatises: Title Record,

Phonetic Glosses, Volume Two; Prolegomenon, Part Two: On the Arising of Dharmas (up to) the Conclusion on the Essential Purpose; Title of the Treatise.
The Treatise Master and Translation Master’s Commentary on the Initial Homage through the End of the Verses, with Phonetic Glossary in Three Volumes.
The Treatise states (up to): "The two gates are not mutually exclusive" (phonetic gloss:
four fascicles).
Regarding "the true suchness of mind" (up to): "it gives rise to all phenomena" (phonetic gloss).

In the fifth fascicle, it asks: "What are the two? The first is the mirror of awakening (up to the end of the section on) the conditioning of objects. [This concludes] the commentary on the *Śrīmālādevī-siṃhanāda-sūtra* in six fascicles.
The phonetic glosses for the section from "That which is called non-awakening" (up to) "the obstruction of wisdom," Volume Seven;
and the phonetic glosses for the section from "Discriminating the characteristics of arising and ceasing" (up to) "the Tathāgata-garbha."
The Explanatory Glossary for Volume Eight, from "The Function of True Suchness" to "Falling into the Stage of the Two Vehicles," Volume Nine.

The *Commentary on the Explanation of Terms for the "Chapter on the Attainment of Faith and the Arousing of the Mind"* (up to the point where both [calm abiding and special insight] manifest simultaneously),
ten fascicles;
and the *Commentary on the Explanation of Terms for the Verses of the Treatise* (up to the end of the verses).

The Collected Readings of the *Commentary and Sub-commentary on the Treatise on the Awakening of Faith* (Qixin lun shuji huoyue) consists of ten volumes in total, arranged in sequential order. Other works,
such as the *External Transmission* (Waike zhuan), have been compiled separately as the first volume for reference.

In the first fascicle, the "Prolegomenon" (*nidāna*) recounts the causes and conditions for the compilation of this edition; thus it stands at the beginning. The "Sectional Analysis" (*vibhāga*) provides a systematic outline of the entire great work; thus it follows next.
The "Five Patriarchs," representing the school’s primary tradition, were first ordered to be compiled in an abbreviated form; thus they occupy the third position.
The two records by the Master of Treatises and the Master of Commentaries were subsequently added as supplements; thus they occupy the fourth position. The Dharma... [text ends]

The "Preface" (xiàng) sets forth the general outline of the treatise; it constitutes the fifth section. The "Diagrammatic Seal" (túzhāng) arranges the essential purport within the treatise and is placed at the end.
As for other digressive and peripheral matters that are not pertinent, they have all been excised and omitted from the record.

Originally, there was one fascicle of topical outlines (*ke-mon*). Following the outlines for the treatise (*ron*), the outlines for the commentary (*sho*) were appended as redundant additions, which I found to be quite distracting.
Now, within these separate topical outlines, I have compiled only those for the treatise; the outlines for the commentary remain within the records.
This not only eliminates redundancy and complexity, but also corresponds most closely with the annotated edition of Guishan.
The Preface by Dai Xu, together with a summary of the general intent of the commentaries and records, should properly precede the volumes;
therefore, it is placed at the beginning of the first fascicle.
In the former editions, the *Śāstra* was divided into four fascicles and the *Commentary* into twenty fascicles.
In the present combined edition, the *Śāstra* and *Commentary* are merged into ten fascicles in total. While the number of fascicles differs considerably, the words and phrases remain no different.
It is like pouring the water from twenty-four bottles into ten; how could there be even a single drop lost in the process?
Is there a difference? Let those with discerning eyes examine this.

From the first fascicle to near the end of the second fascicle, the text is explained according to the original scripture. Words written flush with the top margin are the commentary (*śāstra*), while words marked by being set down one space lower are the annotations (*ṭīkā*).
From the end of the second fascicle following the word-by-word commentary up to the conclusion of the tenth fascicle: those written in the top margin are the *śāstra* (treatise) text;
those marked with the character "shu" (疏) set down one space lower are the *vyākhyā* (commentary) text; and those marked with the character "ji" (記) are the *abhisamaya* (sub-commentary) text.
The division of the text into sections within this treatise follows the structural analysis (*kepan*) established by the Great Master Xianshou; there is no deviation from his arrangement.
The paragraph divisions of the introductory commentary (*xu-shu*) preceding the treatise may be understood by analogy with this.

The structural divisions (kē) are layered upon one another, making it difficult to clarify their origins and development. When Master Jiaoguang categorized the *Śūraṃgama Sūtra*, he innovatively employed the sexagenary cycle (gānzhī).

Now, by following his precedent to mark these divisions, the sequence of the generations—from great-grandfather to grandson—becomes orderly, and the underlying connections between preceding and succeeding sections are likewise rendered coherent.
The textual meanings of the treatise and its commentaries arise in successive order; the same applies to the structural divisions and their analytical explanations. This is like a tree:
first there is a single trunk, which then branches into two, three, four, or five limbs; from the major branches, the intermediate branches emerge.
From among these, minor branches are further divided into groups of two, three, and four; this follows the Yunqi edition in detail,
without omission, so that the beginning and end may correspond with one another, ensuring that those who read and study it do not fall into confusion or error.
The sub-commentary (*ṭīkā*) appended beneath the topical outline (*kośa*), as well as the commentary (*vyākhyā*) appended beneath the treatise (*śāstra*), both follow the edition of Mount Gui;
they differ from the Yunqi edition, which inserts the sub-commentary beneath the topical outline before the commentary itself.

The notation "Commentary on the Sections" (*kehou biaoshu ji*) following a section heading indicates that this is an explanation of the structural divisions of the text. The notation "Commentary on the Treatise" (*lunhou biaoshu ji*) following a treatise passage indicates that one is now explaining the actual content of the treatise.
Fearing that these might be confused with one another, I have set them forth here first.
In the Gui-shan manuscript edition, there are commentaries provided for each sentence; therefore, the commentary does not cite the main text of the treatise.

In the Yun-qi printed edition, the text is divided into sections according to topical headings, and within these sections, the commentary is extensive; logically, the commentary in this version ought to include citations from the main text.
I have now likewise compiled this following the format of the Yunqi edition; however, I have abridged certain phrases and do not agree with it entirely.
In the commentaries of the older editions, there are also passages recorded that do not correspond to the main treatise. I have now corrected these according to the original text.
This is annotated as in the *Commentary on the Four Marks*, which explains "inner awareness regarding the foundations of mindfulness" and "the initial arising of awareness of the mind," and so forth.

In the older versions of the sub-commentary (*shu*), there were those who addressed doubts; they would often set forth the text of these difficult questions directly before the section on resolving doubts.
This, however, was too far removed, making it difficult for readers to fully comprehend. If, instead, these notes were placed beneath the specific sections, it would seem more appropriate.

First the external objections, followed by the explanatory discussion. Although this arrangement is convenient, there is a concern that it might be confused with the text of the interpretive sections (*jieke*).

Therefore, both are now moved to follow the main text of the commentary (*shu*). The pattern is as follows: first, the text of the treatise (*lunwen*) is cited, and second, the doubts and objections are set forth.

When used subsequently for explanation and clarification, the meaning of the text becomes manifest and easy to understand, as is the case with the commentaries on the "Similarity" section and the subsequent resolution of doubts regarding the five consciousnesses. This is precisely what is meant.

Regarding those passages in the *Śāstra* (Sū) that are lengthy and difficult to clarify, the *Commentary* (Jì) first provides a structural analysis (*kēpàn*) and subsequently offers a detailed explanation.
This current edition likewise follows the structural analysis of the *Commentary*, merging the *Śāstra* with the *Commentary*.

Those who study this work must first read the *Śāstra*, next examine the *Commentary* alone, and finally study both the *Śāstra* and the *Commentary* together once through. By repeating this process three times, the purport of the treatise will become self-evident.
Furthermore, the intent of the *Shu* (Commentary) and the *Ji* (Record) is entirely transparent.
Where the text of the *Shu* is brief and that of the *Ji* is extensive, if the meaning can be divided, I shall separate the *Shu* and follow the *Ji*;
if the *Ji* must be integrated with the *Shu*, I shall do so. Even if both the *Shu* and the *Ji* are extensive and the meaning cannot be divided, I dare not arbitrarily make such a partition.
I have torn [the original] because it damaged the continuity of the textual lineage.

Regarding points in the treatise that were not yet categorized, I have recorded them here for further categorization; regarding points that were not yet annotated, I have recorded them here for further explanation.
All of these are now compiled and recorded within this text rather than being listed as separate sections; nevertheless, each maintains its own distinct identity.
Those explaining the *śāstra* (treatise) designate it as "the *śāstra*," while those explaining the *vṛtti* (commentary) designate it as "the *vṛtti*.

Just as with the two characters "treatise" (*lun*) and "commentary" (*shu*), one must invariably cite the full text of the treatise and the complete sentences of the commentary. Those who investigate these matters should naturally pay close attention to this.

In the *Ji* (Commentary), I have already elaborated beyond what was contained in the *Jie-shu* (Explanatory Commentary). Those of superior faculties and sharp intelligence will certainly find it perfectly coherent and unimpeded;

however, those of inferior capacity might otherwise conclude that there are two or three conflicting doctrines. Therefore, within this compiled edition, I have reconciled those points that were excessively divergent.

A brief deletion of one or two phrases (as in the section on Initial Enlightenment [shijue], where the Commentary says: "The seven consciousnesses do not transmigrate," while the Record says: "The Sūtra states that the five consciousnesses do not transmigrate; here it says the seven consciousnesses").

The commentary’s notation was erroneous; this [criticism] was based on the Tang translation. Little did they realize that the commentary relies upon the Song translation—how could it be subject to such criticism? Items of this sort shall be deleted.

Those that are somewhat consistent with the original shall remain unchanged (such as the commentaries on the "Gate of True Suchness" regarding the subduing of attachments, and the "Meeting of Characteristics" regarding their mutual inclusion and reality). This shall ensure that those who study and interpret the text will correctly follow the meaning of the commentary.
Furthermore, one may consult the intent of the records as an aid for clarification.

For when the *Laṅkāvatāra*, the *Awakening of Faith*, and other sutras and śāstras were translated, Master Zang was personally present within the assembly to certify the meaning. How could the resulting commentaries contain errors or discrepancies that would lead to the confusion of later students?
The Master Zang’s commentary consists of three fascicles and his record one fascicle, which were transmitted for those of strong learning.
Guishan, however, produced separate versions of the treatise and the commentary, fearing that those of middling or inferior capacity might not be able to read them all.

He consequently annotated the commentary text beneath the corresponding sections of the treatise, deleting the redundant and extracting the essential, compiling them into two fascicles. Thus, Qingliang’s *Huayan*...

Regarding the various passages from the *Commentary on the Awakening of Faith* (*Qixinlun shuji*) cited within the *Sub-commentary* (*Shuchao*), those not found therein all belong to the Master’s own personal compositions of the *Shuji*, and are not the version of the *Lülu* (Abridged Record) by Guishan nor the record finalized by Changshui.
Read one and do not read the other; do not give rise to doubts or disputes.

The *Śāstra* (treatise) consists of sections comprising headings, interrogations, explanations, and conclusions; the *Vyākhyā* (commentary) provides a general overview of chapters and detailed exegesis of individual sentences;

and the *Ṭīkā* (sub-commentary) distinguishes between its interpretation of the *Śāstra* and its interpretation of the *Vyākhyā*. If one does not [囗-┐]—the character pronounced as "gōu" (hook)—these at the outset, one will remain bewildered.

Now, within the *Śāstra*, *Vyākhyā*, and *Ṭīkā*, there are instances where large sections are [囗-┐]ed and instances where individual sentences are [囗-┐]ed; with a single reading, one will immediately understand the divisions.
I have not allowed any obstructions to remain within the pupils [of the reader].
The original woodblock edition did not mark the *jiùdú* (the points where the text pauses, pronounced *jué* and meaning "vertical") nor did it divide the chapters into sections.
Now, for the benefit of beginners, I have added some marks to facilitate reading and viewing.

The sub-commentary (*shuji*) previously lacked phonetic glosses. Now, at the end of each fascicle, I have added detailed phonetic transcriptions so that there will be no need for further consultation.
Within the circulating versions of the sub-commentary, many characters are erroneous or missing; these are all merely errors from transcription. Now, based upon...
The ancient edition has been augmented and revised; in some instances, corrections have been made according to the meaning.

Wherever the *Shelun shu* (Commentary on the *Mahāyānasaṃparigraha-śāstra*) contains passages that relate to both doctrine and contemplation (*jiaoguan*) and are of vital importance within the Dharma, these have all been extensively polished and explained within the present record.

I have simply compared the two versions—the new and the old, opened and synthesized—once against each other, so that I may know for myself what is gained and lost. Should there be any errors or omissions, I hope [for correction].
I humbly request your compassionate instruction. Regarding the *Exegesis on the Commentary to the Treatise on the Awakening of Faith*, I have compiled this record of its origins.

I have heard that the treatises of the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna distinguish between the fundamental and the derivative, and between essence and appearance; yet, among them all, the *Treatise on the Awakening of Faith* alone... [is the original source].

It encompasses the beginning and concludes with the end; it penetrates both emptiness and existence, serving as the pivotal mechanism for the fundamental and the derivative, and the central knot of nature and characteristics.

Among the five treatises composed by the Great Being Aśvaghoṣa, this one alone is practiced universally; it serves as the reliance for both ordinary beings and sages, and is the synthesis of all dharmas.
The principle of the single vehicle (*ekayāna*), the ultimate reality of dependent origination, and the meaning of the *dharmadhātu* are revealed herein; it is nowhere else to be found.
This treatise exists in two translations. Formerly, Emperor Wu of the Liang dynasty dispatched an envoy to India to seek out scriptures.
At that time, the King of Magadha sent the śramaṇa Kuṇalānanda—whose name was translated as Paramārtha—from the kingdom of Ujjayinī in Western India. This Tripitaka Master endured great hardship...
He declined the invitation, but eventually boarded a boat to come to court. Accompanied by Gautama and many attendants, he presented offerings of *sūhaka* incense and a Buddha image.

By the end of the month, he encountered the disturbances caused by Hou Jing. The Tripiṭaka Master wished to return to his ship, but happened to meet with the eminent worthies of the capital—Hui Xian, Zhi Shao, Tan Zhen, and Hui Min—as well as Xiao Bo, the Grand General of the Yellow Halberd and Grand Guardian (Taibao).

Request: On the tenth day of the ninth month of the third year of the Chengsheng era of the Great Liang dynasty, at Jianxing Monastery in Shixing Commandery, Hengzhou, this treatise in one fascicle was translated, along with the *Xuanwen* (Profound Text) on the Essential Meaning of the Treatise in twenty fascicles, the *Xuanwen* on the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* in four fascicles, the *Sūtra on the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination* in two fascicles, and the *Yizhang on the Nine Consciousnesses* in two fascicles. The interpreter was from Yuezhi.
The scribes Guo Shou-na and others, including Zhi Kai and his colleagues, completed the work over the course of two years.

Subsequently, during the Chang’an era of Empress Wu of the Tang dynasty, the Śramaṇa Śikṣānanda (translated as "Delight in Learning") from the kingdom of Khotan retranslated this treatise at Foshouji Monastery in the Eastern Capital (Luoyang).
It was rendered into two fascicles; Bolun Xuan Gui served as the scribe for the dictation, and Fu Li [served as the proofreader].
Regarding the composition of the text: Master Huìlǎng [compiled] the *Fǎbǎofǎzàngděng zhèngyì* (Verification of the Meaning of the Dharma-Jewel Treasury).

The National Teacher Xuánzhòu, while participating in the translation assembly for the two translations—specifically the Tang translation—feared that [the commentary] might involve partiality; therefore, he specifically interpreted the Liáng dynasty version, producing three volumes of sub-commentary (*shū*) and one volume of a separate record (*biéjì*).
Because that record was somewhat brief, Dharma Master Shíbì further integrated its essential meanings and composed a separate extensive record, which has been transmitted.

Practitioners weary of its prolixity; thus, the Great Master Changshui re-examined the sutras and śāstras, further refining and augmenting the text to achieve a middle way, thereby avoiding the faults of either excess or deficiency.
In the year Kāngxī Yǐsī (1705), while I was at Lianju, I listened to the Dharma-elder Lingcang lecture on this treatise.
By minutely studying the text and the underlying intent of the commentaries and records, I came to truly understand the wisdom of the Third Patriarch, Xianshou.
The National Preceptor established his school and judged the teachings, elucidating the ultimate depths of the three vehicles’ sudden and gradual approaches;
all of this relies upon this treatise. In the autumn of the Wumu year, Mr. Dai Fuzhai, Vice-Governor of Shuntian Prefecture, exhorted me to produce a commentary on the treatise.
During the summer of the Jiwu year, when I began lecturing on the exposition, the gentleman printed and distributed over one hundred copies of the treatise, along with his own private annotations.
The Preface states: "My entry into the Way was truly due to this commentary on the treatise as the initial cause for awakening.
Reading it quietly, I first believed that the reason the Master chose to dwell among the forests and springs was that his aspirations lay solely in the Buddha-dharma.

Less than two months later, I extracted the essential points and composed two fascicles of a summary. When the Master saw them, he immediately ordered someone to transcribe them and store them within a chest.
In the tenth month, the Master took his four volumes of commentaries (*shu*) and twenty volumes of records (*ji*), each of which had been bound as separate fascicles and had not yet been punctuated.

As scholars found it difficult to consult them, he again commissioned me to produce a combined edition of the commentaries and records, requiring that the sections and paragraphs be clearly demarcated with punctuation in accordance with their logical order.
The subheadings (*ke*) and annotations were to be placed within the commentary text itself, each in its proper position. I, reflecting upon the lineage of the House of the Sages...

I acknowledge this. Among the ten great commentaries, it is solely upon this section that we rely for its preservation. Now, having added the *Fenbie* (Distinction) chapter, the original intent is fully realized.
Consequently, I began compiling it on the eighth day of the twelfth month; by the beginning of the twentieth, the draft of the first fascicle was completed, and I went to present it for correction.

The Master, filled with boundless joy and praise, commanded that the remaining nine fascicles follow this established standard. On the eleventh day of the new year in the Gengshen year, he again sent [the instructions].
I read the two-fascicle draft and likewise granted my approval. On the twelfth day of the second month, I met regarding the three fascicles;

on the third day of the third month, the four fascicles; on the twenty-fifth, the five fascicles; on the sixteenth day of the fourth month, the six fascicles; on the twenty-sixth, the seven fascicles;
on the tenth day of the fifth month, the eight fascicles; on the nineteenth, the nine fascicles; and on the third day of the sixth month, the ten fascicles.

*Juan* (Volumen). *Dingke wen* (Text on the Eleven Fixed Rules), one fascicle. *Shu zhuzu lueji* (Brief Record of the Various Patriarchs), composed on the first day of the seventh month, one fascicle.
On the Buddha’s Day of Joy during the Zhongyuan festival, the diagrams of the Dharma characteristics were drawn and the compilation was completed.

After the thirteenth day of the first month of the Xinyou year, the Master unexpectedly fell slightly ill. On the twenty-seventh day of the second month, he wrote the "Private Commentary" (*Zisi zhu*).
[The Master] said: "I have devoted my mind to this matter, yet I regret that I did not fulfill my ambition. My understanding was thorough, but I failed to put it into practice.
It is fortunate that you, Dharma Master, shall enlighten others with this; you must ensure that it is brought into actual practice. Having finished the preface, he entrusted it to Mr.

Chang Renchang, saying: "Deliver this commentary to the Dharma Master. You should have the original text carved for printing and circulation. Do not let your poverty be a source of bitterness, nor fail me by neglecting this task."

"Long have I yearned for this. On the twenty-eighth day, early in the morning, he wrote a verse on departing from the world, saying: 'I originally studied the Chan of Tiantai And had already reached the second or third stage.
I further investigated the Chan beyond the teachings, And was nearly close to shattering the void. The bitterness of official service entangled me, Preventing me from fulfilling this resolve.
Today I cast off my hands and return; Where, then, shall my traces remain? At the hour of the rat on the twenty-ninth, he spoke to his relatives."

He said: "In this life I am unable to leave the household life and have not attained meditative concentration; I vow that in a future life I shall become a monk and swiftly realize the fruit of enlightenment.
You may take my dharma robe, meditation robe, staff, and prayer beads and place them at my side. At noon yesterday, a monk arrived from Tianmu;
at this moment, you must invite him to the Buddha Hall to chant the Buddha’s name aloud to assist my right mindfulness. (1)
"All worldly affairs are like illusions and dreams; meeting must inevitably lead to parting. Do not weep at all.
Having finished these instructions, he recited the Buddha’s name more than a thousand times. He then asked for the time and took his leave of the assembly, passing away with serene composure.

On the first day of the fifth month of the following year, the Renxu year, his eldest son gathered skilled artisans and entrusted the work to the carvers within the Seven Buddhas Hall in the rear garden.
In the eighth month of the year Yi-chu (1625), [the project] was moved to the Hall of Ciyun Monastery;
by the seventh month of Ding-mao (1627), the carving of the woodblocks was completed. Thus, the publication of this scripture was indeed a matter of great significance.

I recall that on the fourteenth night of the ninth month in the autumn of Yi-wei (1619), I dreamed of a man wearing a cloth cap and a headband, appearing like Zhuge Liang (Wuhou), who claimed to be the Teacher of the Heavenly Emperor.

As he ascended the seat to preach the Dharma, humans and devas surrounded him in protection, while fragrant flowers swirled about. Suddenly, he sent a person wearing a jeweled necklace to exhort a certain deity, saying:

"This is the *Qixinlun Shuji* (Commentary on the Awakening of Faith), the treatise of the Teacher of the Heavenly Emperor. You are a deity of merit; you ought to receive it upon the crown of your head and practice accordingly.
That deity immediately conferred the book upon him, saying: "The Master has sent me to entrust this to you. I bowed and received it with reverence.
Furthermore, he saw eight golden characters inscribed upon the surface of the book, which read: "The Supreme Lord is present before you; do not let your heart be divided.
He then correlated these with the signs of his former dream: the one wrapped in a turban was the Venerable Patriarch Xianshou;

the one wearing a jeweled crown was the Great Master Changshui; and the one of celestial merit was the Master Fuzhai. The *Shuji* (Commentary) refers to the *Huiben* (Collected Editions). "Do not let your heart be divided" is a word of admonition.
This is a virtuous deed that has been taken to heart by the Celestial Emperor. How could it be said that such a subtle affinity and minor matter were possible?
Were it not for the accumulation of virtuous vows over many lifetimes, how could one have received such a dream-omen in advance?

Were it not for receiving the Dharma-seal of the Spirit Mountain (Vulture Peak), how could one maintain such clarity of awareness while departing and dwelling? Regarding your question about the Master’s inquiry into the Dharma with the Elder of Plum Valley—this is not so.
He was no different from the Duke Ou-yang Wen-tung in his realization;

he received the transmission from Master Tianmu, no different from Wang the Attendant of Xiangzhou in his cessation of delusion and transformation of karma; he practiced tranquility and cultivated insight, no different from Minister Wen;
he protected and supported the Buddhist gate, no different from Prefect Pei; and he published the scriptural teachings, no different from Prime Minister Fang.

He was a true statesman. To request a commentary on the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* was no different from the Secretariat Director Zheng. To abridge the *Cīvaravastu* of the *Vinaya* was no different from the Court Scholar of the Liang dynasty.
His final testament, which directed that robes of the "ruined color" (badara-vastra) be placed within his coffin, was no different from that of the Duke Wenzheng Dan.
As for the entire family’s faith and inclination toward the Buddha-dharma, it was no different from that of Layman Pang and his son. From this day forward, one must believe in this treatise.
Now that this commentary has been obtained for wide dissemination, and the gateways to cultivation and realization have been clarified,
what cause for concern is there that the doctrinal net of Aśvaghoṣa and Xianshou might be torn asunder? I am truly filled with joy at the ultimate fulfillment of this great merit,
and thus I record its origins and conclusion at the beginning of this volume.

A Brief Record of the Five Patriarchs of the Dharmadhātu School, Preface.
In the summer of the Gengshen year, while I was at the Seven Buddhas Hall, I was perusing the Tripiṭaka and examining the history of the monastic community.

One day, I inquired of Dharma Master Baiting of Ciyun regarding the five patriarchs of the Avataṃsaka school. Upon hearing his explanation, I privately harbored some doubts, and therefore requested further instruction.

Before even ten days had passed since the compilation of the *Biographies of the Five Patriarchs*, the Dharma Master compiled a single volume titled *Brief Record*. Upon examining it, it became clear that the ecclesiastical histories were indeed inconsistent and erroneous.

For instance, regarding the Third Patriarch, the Great Master Xianshou, the tradition states that in the Bingshen year of the Dengfeng era, an imperial decree ordered the Master to lecture on the new sutra;

moved by this, his mouth emitted light and the earth shook, whereupon the Emperor issued an edict for the Ten Virtuous Ones to confer the precepts upon him. Now, let us examine this according to the present record.
The new scripture was only translated during the Yiwu year of the Zhengsheng era; it was completed only at the beginning of the Jihai year of the Shenglì era.

How could it have been lectured upon before it had even been translated? Moreover, the Third Patriarch received the tonsure in the Gengwu year of the Xianheng era and began lecturing immediately upon receiving the imperial decree.
By the Bingshen year of the Dengfeng era—twenty-seven years later—the Patriarch was fifty-four years old and his Way had filled the world, only then [did he...]
To claim that he received the precepts is logically untenable. Furthermore, the *Huan-yuan guan* (Contemplation of Returning to the Source) has been falsely attributed to the Venerable Du-shun.
Since the National Preceptor’s lifespan ended at seventy, if this [claim] were true, the errors in the historical records would be all too evident.
Later, I further investigated the original sources of the *Lüji* (Abridged Record). It states: "The first and second patriarchs produced the *Huìxuán*; the third patriarch detailed the *Cūizhuàn*;
and the fourth and fifth patriarchs recorded them in various commentaries. Upon examining these, there was not the slightest discrepancy.

Indeed, the Buddha transmitted the Dharma of the mind to the successive patriarchs, and the patriarchs propagated this Dharma of the mind throughout the Dharma-realm; thus, until the end of the future, their transformation and edification shall never cease. Its...
Can the traces of the Way be without evidence? Without evidence, people will not believe; and if they do not believe, how can they emulate them?

Is it not for this reason that there is a need for the patriarchs and Buddhas? From this day forward, let it be known that the upholding and nurturing of the Buddha-dharma depends entirely upon the patriarchs, and the learning of the patriarchal Way depends entirely upon the canonical records. Thus, this record is no small contribution.
He then ordered it to be carved so that it might be shared with all who appreciate it.
May those who see or hear it and rejoice therein take care not to dismiss it as superfluous talk. Inscribed by the layman Dai Jingzeng of Fuzhai in Hulin.

The First Patriarch, Venerable Dushun:
The First Patriarch’s name was Fashun. His imperial posthumous title was Dixin. His secular surname was Du, and he was a native of Duling in Wannian County, Yongzhou.
He was born in the second year of the Yongding era of Emperor Wu of the Chen dynasty. When he was only three days old, a wet nurse came of her own accord to seek him out.

He was nourished [by his parents] until he reached three months of age, at which point he ascended into the air and departed (1). During his childhood, he frequently preached the Dharma upon a burial mound behind his house;
those who heard him were all moved to faith and awakening, and for this reason the mound was named "The Mound of Preaching the Dharma" (2).

At the age of fifteen, he took over the leadership of his elder brother’s army to suppress rebels. He provided more than sufficient supplies of water and firewood for a host of one hundred thousand soldiers. One night, he secretly...

The Master personally shaved his head and beard; at that time, the earth shook, and the Earth Deity held out a basin to receive [the falling hair].

There was none who could not be transformed. When the fast was concluded, the five hundred people were transformed into arhats and departed on clouds (5).
Zhang Hongchang kept oxen and horses that were extremely vicious by nature; yet he showed them such kindness and compassion that they no longer gored or bit him (6).

Later, when he led the assembly to Mount Li to dwell in seclusion, he intended to plant vegetables. As the ground was infested with many insects and ants, he then circled its boundaries to establish the demarcation, whereupon the insects [ceased their activity].
He moved to the outskirts, where he was able to cultivate the land without harm (7). He still suffered from a swelling that oozed pus externally.
When someone washed it with water, the fragrance was incomparable; when others wiped it with silk, the aroma did not dissipate. Soon he recovered, and he would help others eliminate swellings (8).
A man named Tian Sadāpura from San Yuan County had been deaf since birth; when called to him, he was immediately able to hear.

(9) Furthermore, one Zhang Su also suffered from a congenital inability to speak; upon being addressed by [the Master], he was immediately able to speak (10). A monk in Wengong County was possessed by a venomous dragon.

When the assembly sought his aid, [the Master] sat facing him with hands folded in formal composure. The dragon then spoke through the monk, saying: "Now that the Chan Master has arrived, it is right that I do not remain for long.
Shortly thereafter, the affliction was relieved (11). Thus, the pestilences and malignant influences of far and near were [subdued].

As for those afflicted by vexations, there was none who did not seek his help; yet he would not employ other arts, but instead directed them toward meditative contemplation (*dhyāna*), and there were none whose ailments were not healed.
Even sacred trees and dragon temples he would see and immediately destroy; as for the objects of worship for shamans and sorcerers, he personally eliminated them.
The people of the world all marveled at him, calling him the "Dunhuang Bodhisattva" (12). From this, his fame reached the imperial court during the Sui dynasty. Emperor Wen...

The Emperor placed great faith and reverence in him, providing him with a monthly stipend for his support (13). Later, while traveling to the Southern Mountains, he encountered the flooding of the River Hengqu.
His attendants were struck with fear, but Daoxang led the group across together; the water immediately ceased its flow, and they passed through with measured steps.

As soon as they reached the bank, the water returned to its former state (14). At that time, during a ritual alms-round for a feast, the host of the meal was holding an infant and requested that his misfortunes be dispelled and his life-span extended.
Shang looked at him intently and said, "This is your enemy; you must repent before him. When the meal was finished, Shang ordered him to carry the child to the riverbank and threw it into the water.

Internally and externally, his deportment and ritual observances were like those of a Buddha (20). It is nothing but the true realm. It has no form or appearance, yet it pervades the great trichiliocosm; it has no boundaries, yet it contains all phenomena.
It is luminously clear within the mind and eyes, yet its form cannot be seen; it shines brilliantly amidst the objects of sensory dust, yet its principle cannot be divided.
Without the eye of wisdom that penetrates all dharmas and the brilliant intelligence that is free from conceptual thought, one cannot perceive it.
One's own mind is thus so wondrous and penetrating. Therefore, when the World-Honored One first attained perfect enlightenment, he exclaimed, "How marvelous!
I now see that all sentient beings universally possess the wisdom, virtue, and marks of a Tathāgata; yet, due to deluded thoughts and attachments, they are unable to realize it.
Thereupon, in accordance with the nature of the Dharma-realm, he preached the Avataṃsaka Sūtra, which is entirely based on true emptiness.
Discerning emotion, he realized the fusion of principle and phenomena; all-pervasive and profoundly still—this is what is called the Great Tenet of the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*).

After Emperor Di had listened to this profound discourse, he attained a state of vast clarity and realization. He immediately issued an edict to the relevant authorities to cast a special golden seal and conferred upon him the title of State Preceptor Qingliang, the Unifier of Monks.
He was thus authorized to preside over the monastic community throughout the empire and to oversee the affairs of the Buddhist gate (29). [The reigns of] Emperors Muzong and Jingzong followed.
All looked up to his immense merit. He was posthumously bestowed the title of State Preceptor Dazhao (30).

In the fifth year of the Tahe era of Emperor Wenzong, the Emperor received the mind-precepts from the Master and vowed never to eat clams (31). In the first year of the Kaicheng era, the Emperor celebrated the Master’s hundredth birthday.
He was granted robes, wealth, food, and delicacies; he was conferred the title of Grand State Preceptor (32); he lectured on the Great Sūtras fifty times in their entirety (33);
he established fifteen Unrestricted Great Assemblies (34); and as for his writings that have been transmitted to the present day:

In total, there are over four hundred fascicles. Chancellor Qi Kang, Zheng Yuying, and Gao Ying requested that he compose the *Huayan Gangyao* (Essential Outlines of the Avataṃsaka) in three fascicles.
Chancellor Li Jifu, Vice Minister Gui Deng, Fu Ma, and Du Cong requested that he write the *Zhengyao* (Essential Points) in one fascicle.
Grand Marshal Gao Chongwen requested that he author the *Jingdeng Shuowen* (Exposition on the Mirror-Lamp) in one fascicle. Minister of Works Yan Rou and Minister of Works [Sikong]...
Zheng Yuan; the Provincial Inspector Lu Changyuan, who requested the compilation of one scroll titled *The Contemplation on the Perfect Fusion of the Three Sages*;
the Military Governor Xue Hua; the Surveillance Commissioner Meng Jian; Qian Hui of the Secretariat; the Palace Attendant Bai Juyi; Du Gao of the Department of State Affairs, and others.

He requested the production of the "Diagram of the Flower Treasury World" (*Huazangjie tu*) based on the seven locations and nine assemblies, as well as the ten-fascicle *Xinjing Shuowen* (Exegesis on the Mirror of the Mind).

Furthermore, together with the Chief Registrar of Monks, Grand Master Ling Sui; the eighteen head seats; and the eminent practitioners of the three studies from ten monasteries, he compiled more than thirty works concerning the essential principles of the *Avataṃsaka*, *圆觉* (*Yuánjué*), *四分* (*Sifen*), and *中观* (*Zhongguan*) scriptures, vinayas, and śāstras. He also composed the *Dajing Liaoyi Bei* (Supplement to the Definitive Meaning of the Great Scripture).

He authored three volumes of the *Discourse on the Scripture Explained before the Emperor on the Festival of the Seven Sages’ Descent*, as well as over eighty volumes of poetry, notes, and official correspondence from his own school (35).
Among his disciples who became teachers themselves, there were thirty-eight, headed by Hǎi'àn and Jìguāng;
those who received his instruction numbered one thousand, including Sēngruì of Tōngjīng and Zōngmì of Guishān.
He alone attained its profound mysteries; all others came with empty hearts and departed with full bellies (36).

On the sixth day of the third month in the third year of the Kaicheng era, he summoned his senior disciples, including the Chief Seat of the Three Teachings, Master Baoyin Hai'an, and others, and entrusted them with these words:
I have heard that the ancients lamented the futility of relying on mere chance, and that the sages of old were ashamed of those who lacked essential substance.

There is no distinction between the ancestral order of *zhāomù* or the movements of stillness; there is no thread of continuity in the cycle of coming and going. Do not engage in the excavation of heterodox views; do not follow what is wrong or argue for the false.

Do not allow your minds to become lost in or ensnared by depravity; do not stubbornly cling to strife. Even the Great Illumination cannot dispel the darkness of the long night, nor can a compassionate mother—
"To ensure the safety of your offspring after your passing, you should place your trust in the Buddha and not in man. The True Realm is profound and subtle;
it is not revealed through words and speech, but must be realized through deep resolve. When it manifests clearly before you, you will have no mind toward objects and remain unmoved by circumstances.
If you do so, you shall not bring me to grief. Having finished speaking, he sat in the lotus posture and passed away. (37) The Master’s life spanned nine...

In the morning, he served as the Preceptor to seven emperors. His secular age was one hundred and two; his monastic seniority (*saṃgha-lakṣa*) was eighty-three. His discourse was refined and elegant, and his deportment served as a model for others.

In learning, he surveyed the nine schools of thought; in talent, he could match the two brushes (of the scribe). He observed the practice of eating only once throughout his life and did not store away any surplus provisions (38).
Emperor Wenzong, out of profound reverence for this ancestral sage, specifically suspended court for three days, and his high ministers wore white mourning garments (39). [He] shed his mortal coil.

After twenty-one days, his countenance became even more radiant and moist. He sat upright with a majesty as imposing as a mountain. On the twenty-seventh day of that month, by imperial decree, his entire body was enshrined in a stupa on Mount Zhongnan.

During the first anniversary of his passing, a monk from India arrived at the capital and submitted a memorial stating that he had seen two messengers crossing the Pamir Mountains while soaring through the air. He was a deity of the Mañjuśrī Hall in North India. From the Eastern Land (China), he took a great tooth of the Avataṃsaka Bodhisattva and returned to his country to offer it in worship.
By imperial decree, the stupa was opened to verify this; indeed, one tooth had vanished, and only thirty-nine remained.

They were brilliantly white like frost, and their features appeared as if alive. Subsequently, he was cremated, and several thousand grains of śarīra were obtained, which were luminous, clear, and lustrous.

In the second year of the Yuanhe era of Emperor Xianzong, as he was about to go to the capital to take the imperial examinations, he happened to meet Daoyuan of Dayun Temple in Suizhou.

He attained great enlightenment. His body and mind leaped with joy, and he returned to report this to Yuán. Yuán said, "The Buddhas have transmitted this scripture to you.

While Lingfeng was ill, he bestowed upon him the twenty fascicles of the *Great Commentary on the Avataṃsaka Sūtra* and the forty fascicles of the *Great Compendium* composed by National Teacher Qingliang.

Upon meeting Yuánjué, my mind and heart were opened at a single word; within this single scroll, the sky of meaning shone with brilliant clarity.
Now, having further obtained this Great Dharma, how fortunate I am! He then preached it once for the assembly. (6) The sixth year of the Yuánhé era.
He traveled to the Eastern Capital to pay homage at the ancestral pagodas and stayed at Yongmu Temple. At the repeated request of the fourfold assembly, he lectured for a second time.

From afar, he recounted the etiquette of his disciples and dispatched the attendants Xuanguī and Zhìhuī to deliver the memorial to the Master. The Master immediately issued a reply, stating:

"Without meeting in person and without oral transmission, you have grasped my intent through this written expression. That your understanding is identical to my own heart—this has never occurred before.

It is not by relying on saintly power alone, but must surely depend upon past causes; you may be compared to a true son of a Wheel-Turning King. If we were to meet face-to-face, it would serve as a seal of confirmation."
"His bonds were already severed; what more could be added? (8) When the lectures concluded, he went to the capital to pay his respects to the State Preceptor Qingliang.
The Master said, "As for the Vairocana-flower Treasury, who else but you could follow me on this journey? For the first two years, he attended upon him day and night.

After several years of seeking further instruction, in the spring of the eleventh year of the Yuanhe era, while at Zhiju Temple on Mount Zhongnan, he produced the *Yuanjue kewen* (Outline of the Perfect Enlightenment Sutra) and the *Zuanyao* (Essential Compendium) in two fascicles. He vowed not to descend from the mountain and spent three years reading the entire Tripitaka.
His vows were fulfilled. In the fourteenth year, at Xingfu Temple, he produced one fascicle of the *Vajrasamādhi-sūtra-śāstra-ṭīkā* and one fascicle of its *Vyākhyā* (12).
In the spring of the fifteenth year, at both Xingfu and Baoshou Temples in the Capital, he compiled two fascicles of the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra-ṭīkā* (13).
In the first year of the Changqing era, he retired to Caotang Temple in Huxian (14). In the spring of the second year, he re-edited the *Mahāyāna-śrīmālā-devī-siṃhanāda-nirdeśa-sūtra*.
In his *Jingjie* (Exegesis on the Sūtras), he further composed the *Huayan lünguan* (The Threaded Summary of the Avataṃsaka) in five fascicles at Fungdoksa Temple on Mount Nanshan (15).
In the summer of the third year, he compiled the *Sifenlü shu* (Commentary on the Dharmaguptaka Vinaya) in three fascicles at Fungdoksa Temple (16).

By the beginning of winter, his work on the *Yuánjué* (Complete Enlightenment) was completed, consisting of the *Dàshǔ* (Great Commentary) in three fascicles and the *Dàchão* (Great Sub-commentary) in thirteen fascicles (17). Subsequently, he also wrote the *Lüeshǔ* (Brief Commentary) in two fascicles and the *Xiǎoshǔ* (Small Commentary).
The *Chao* (Commentary) in six fascicles; the *Daochang Xiuzheng Yi* (Ritual for Cultivation and Realization in the Dharma Hall) in eighteen fascicles (18).

In the second year of the Taihe era, on the anniversary of the Emperor’s birthday, Emperor Wenzong summoned him to the inner palace and inquired about the essentials of all dharmas. He was granted a purple robe and bestowed with the imperial title of "Dade" (Great Virtue) (19).

Court officials, scholars, and commoners alike all looked up to him in reverence; only the Chancellor Pei Xiu penetrated deeply into the inner sanctum and served as his external protector (20). The mountain...
Minister Nán Wēn-zào asked: "For one who has awakened to the principle and stilled delusion, karma is no longer formed.
After the end of this single lifetime, upon what does their numinous spirit rely? The Master said: "All sentient beings are without exception possessed of the nature of awakening.

Its numinous clarity and empty stillness are no different from those of a Buddha. It is only because, since beginningless kalpas, they have never attained realization that they falsely cling to the body as the self."
Because of these appearances, one gives rise to emotions such as love and hatred; following these emotions, one creates karma; following that karma, one receives retribution.

Thus, one undergoes birth, old age, sickness, and death, cycling through saṃsāra for long kalpas. Yet, the enlightened nature within the body has never been born or died. It is like being driven and enslaved in a dream, while the body itself remains fundamentally at ease;
it is like water in a pond turning to ice, while its moist nature does not change. If one can awaken to this nature, it is itself the Dharma.

The body is fundamentally unborn from the beginning; how could it have any basis for reliance? Although the ultimate truth may be realized instantaneously, deluded emotions are difficult to eliminate all at once.
One must constantly maintain awareness, diminishing and further diminishing [delusions]. One should take emptiness and stillness as one’s own essence and not identify with the physical body;
one should take spiritual awareness as one’s own mind and not identify with deluded thoughts. If deluded thoughts arise, do not follow them at all. Thus, [one attains liberation].
At the moment of death, karma can no longer bind one. Although there is an intermediate state (*antarābhava*), one’s destination is free;
one may take up residence at will among the heavens or the human realm. If thoughts of love and hatred have already been extinguished, one will not receive a body of segmented existence.

If the subtle flow of consciousness becomes tranquil and ceases, then the great wisdom of perfect enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-jñāna*) shines forth clearly, manifesting transformations according to the capacities of beings. This is called...
The Buddha spoke in verse: "To perform deeds that are meaningful is the awakened mind; To perform deeds that are meaningless is the deluded mind.
The deluded follow after emotional attachments, And at the moment of death, are dragged away by karma. The awakened do not follow emotions; At the moment of death, they can transform their karma.

(21) [He] subsequently composed commentaries and sub-commentaries on various sutras and treatises, including the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*, the *Śraddhotpāda-śāstra* (Awakening of Faith), the *Bhadracarī-praṇidhāna*, and the *Dharmadhātu-vibhāga*.

He compiled the *Chanyuan quan* (Verification of the Source of Chan), which gathered the Chan teachings of various schools, along with his letters, verses, and discourses, totaling over ninety volumes (22).

On the sixth day of the first month in the first year of the Huichang era of Emperor Wuzong, at Xingfu Monastery, he instructed his disciples to carry his corpse away to be offered to birds and beasts, and for his bones to be cremated and scattered. Having finished speaking, he sat and passed away (23).
On the twenty-second day of that month, the clergy and laity enshrined his whole body at Mount Guifeng for cremation.
Several dozen śarīras were obtained, all white and lustrous. After the fire had subsided, the disciples wept as they searched for them, finding them all within the ashes and embers.
He then concealed [the relics] in a stone chamber (24). He had spent sixty-two years in the world and thirty-four years as a monk.

Among his disciples—the fourfold assembly of monks and nuns—those who attained liberation numbered several thousand. The Chancellor Pei Xiu composed the inscription for his stele, which states in brief:
"The single mind is the totality of all dharmas. When divided, it becomes meditative concentration and wisdom; when expanded, it becomes the six perfections. It continues: "Dispersed..."
Thus one practices the myriad deeds. These myriad deeds have never been anything other than the one mind, and the one mind has never contradicted the myriad deeds.

Therefore, when a Chan Master cultivates the Way, he takes insight and vision as his gateway to the Dharma, takes profound stillness as its true flavor, takes compassion and patience as his armor, and takes wisdom and severance as his sword and spear.
He pacifies and subdues the heterodox and the mixed, and unties the bonds of the cage. Yet the impoverished son does not return; the poor...
That women do not attain prosperity—this my Master deems a shame. That the Three Vehicles do not flourish and the Fourfold Assembly do not prosper—this my Master deems a shame.

That loyalty and filial piety are not cultivated together, and that the burden of responsibility cannot be sustained—this my Master deems a shame. Therefore, he is resolute in rescuing and uplifting others, and earnest in opening the way for and guiding them.
He does not exalt himself on account of a single practice, nor does he tower above others because of a single virtue. When people take refuge in him...
He went to others without waiting for an invitation; when there were those seeking further benefit, he would initiate instruction before they had even reached a state of spiritual fervor.
Though they were children, he did not treat them with disregard in his reception of them; though they were arrogant and headstrong, he never grew weary of exhorting and encouraging them.
Is he not truly a Bodhisattva entrusted by the Tathāgata, a virtuous friend to sentient beings who do not even ask for one? Is he not one of the Four Reliances? Is he not a person of the Ten Stages?

(25) During the reign of Emperor Xuanzong, he was posthumously honored with the title Chan Master Dinghui. His stupa was named Qinglian. (26) These details are recorded at length in other collections.

A Brief Biography of the Master of Treatises, Bodhisattva Aśvaghoṣa.
This Bodhisattva was a native of Central India, from the kingdom of Vārāṇasī. His father’s name was Rūka and his mother’s name was Guṇā.
Six hundred years after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, he manifested his birth (1). At the time of his initial descent from heaven, he moved all the horses to neigh incessantly;
thus he was named Aśvaghoṣa (Horse-Neigher). He was also called Guṇasena (Victorious in Merit), because among all conditioned and unconditioned merits, he was preeminent.

Because it is the most supreme (2). Before he had left the household life, having heard that the Venerable Pūrṇaśa’s realization of the Way was profound and his insight far-reaching, he went to him and said, "Śramaṇa, regarding worldly discourse, I can destroy it like hail crushing grass;
if you submit, I shall cut out your tongue. The Venerable replied slowly, "Within the teachings of all Buddhas, nothing is found outside the Two Truths."
According to conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), one is provisionally designated as a "self. According to ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), all things are entirely empty and quiescent.

When investigated in this manner, how could a self be found? You should reflect upon which of these two is truly superior. Thus did Aśvaghoṣa think in his mind regarding the provisional nature of conventional truth.
"Ultimate emptiness (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*)—since these two truths are thus ungraspable, how can they be destroyed? I have fallen into defeat.
He then bowed his head in apology for his submission (3). The Venerable One ordained him and said to the great assembly: "This Great Being..."
In the past, he was the king of Vaiśālī. There was a class of people who were like naked horses;
the king, employing his supernatural powers, divided his body into silkworms so that the people might obtain clothing. Later, the king was reborn within the borders of Central India;

both the people and the horses were filled with such affection and longing that they neighed piteously, and for this reason he was named Aśvaghoṣa (Horse-Neigh). In the Mahāmāyā Sūtra, the Tathāgata gave this prophecy: "After my parinirvāṇa..."
Six hundred years hence, various non-Buddhists will compete to give rise to false views and destroy the Buddha-dharma.
There will be a bhikṣu named Aśvaghoṣa who excels in expounding the essentials of the Dharma, delivering immeasurable people, and subduing all non-Buddhists with their false views;
now is precisely that time. Furthermore, after [the candidate] has been tonsured and ordained, the Venerable One will again use his supernormal powers to transform and awaken him.

He first placed a sutra in a dark room and immediately had him retrieve it. The man said, "The room is dark; I cannot see. He was told, "If you can simply walk toward it, why worry about not being able to see?
He then used his divine light to illuminate everything, both large and small. The man thought, "This is a magical illusion," and employed every skill at his disposal to dispel it.
Yet the radiance only became twice as intense. Only then did he realize that the Venerable One’s finger-light was blazing forth, and his mind attained clarity.

It was disseminated among humanity to extinguish all darkness and ignorance. The various worthy sages guarded and entrusted it, and it subsequently reached me.

He annotated one hundred Mahāyāna sūtras, including the *Śrīmālādevī-siṃhanāda*, *Prabhāsa*, *Mahāsaṃnipāta*, *Laṅkāvatāra*, *Ratnakūṭa*, *Prajñāpāramitā*, *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, and *Mahāparinirvāṇa*.

Sentient beings of superior, middling, and inferior faculties all entered the Dharma-realm. Among the fourfold assembly, those who saw or heard him gave rise to faith, accepted the teachings, and attained liberation; their number was beyond counting.
Number. In the kingdom of Pāṭaliputra, the local custom esteemed music and dance. [The Buddha] consequently composed a musical piece named Rāḍhāvilāsa to transform the people.

He took seven horses and cut off their water and fodder; after seven days had passed, he gathered the śramaṇas from both within and without [the palace].

Thereupon, the king and his ministers prostrated themselves, and the heretics and outsiders were moved to submit their hearts. (13) Later, he returned once more to the kingdom of Pāṭaliputra and turned the Great Wheel of Dharma. Suddenly, there was...
